doc.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Hearing Marsalis's theme on the radio and playing the same phrase as Wes Anderson
summary: Gordon tells of a Marsalis theme appearing almost identically in a guitarist's radio performance, and of him and Wes Anderson playing the same phrase at a New Orleans jam session.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: somewhere on the west coast, some small rural town out in the midwest. And one of the themes that he wrote [scats] and on the radio we was listening to a jazz station, we had about twenty minutes to get to the sound check, and a guitarist comes on playing [scats]. I said okay, well the first four measures, well I was just hearing the same thing. And then he played the next, and again we hadn’t recorded the music, and this was recorded because it was on the radio. And it was almost exactly identical to what Wynton had written. And we all just looked at each other in the van. I said man it’s wild how this music thing happens. Because there was no correlation between the two, between Wynton and whoever this person was. And then we saw him so I said, “You’re not going to believe this, this was one segment from a piece that you had written, and it was almost exactly note for note, chord change for chord change, the same thing.” So I learned from my experience that when I hear some music if I don’t have music paper I’ll make staff and I’ll just write it down, or enough of it to where I’ll know when I come back to it what frame of mind I was in. And also from the experience of listening to that piece of music that was reminiscent of something that Wynton had done. I say man it’s strange how things just work in the world of music, or just how music moves around. And one last quick thing, I was at a jam session with Wes Anderson in New Orleans and Wynton’s band hadn’t been together. He stopped in September or December of 1995. So this was like ’96, ’97. And they were playing a blues on the stage, Victor Goines was improvising and Wes picked up his horn and I picked up my horn at the same time and were just going to play a background. And we were coming in at the same time [scats]. And we looked at each other. Because we both heard — like we were both hearing the same thing. And Wynton used to talk about that with one of the guys that was in the band one time with Todd Williams, how sometimes we will not just wind up on the same note but end up playing the same phrase. And we’ll just like look at each other and say who did that.
